title: Chapter 5: Quantum Numbers and Electron Configuration — ASC0304 Chemistry I

questions.q: A student proposes the following set of four quantum numbers for an electron: n = 3, ℓ = 2, m_ℓ = -2, mₛ = +½. Determine whether this set is VALID or INVALID. If it is invalid, state clearly which rule is broken and correct the erroneous value.
questions.answer:
VALID.

ell ≤ n - 1: 2 ≤ 2 ✓ - ell ≤ mell ≤ + ell: - 2 ≤ - 2 ≤ + 2 ✓

ms = +½, which is one of the two permitted values (+½ or −½). All four quantum numbers obey the rules, so this is a physically allowed description of an electron.

questions.q: A student proposes the following set of four quantum numbers for an electron: n = 2, ℓ = 2, m_ℓ = 0, mₛ = -½. Determine whether this set is VALID or INVALID. If it is invalid, state clearly which rule is broken and correct the erroneous value.
questions.answer:
INVALID — the rule ℓ ≤ n − 1 is broken.

Rule: ell ≤ n - 1. Given n = 2: ell ≤ 1. But ell = 2 > 1 → INVALID

Correction: the largest permissible ℓ for n = 2 is ℓ = 1 (giving mℓ values from −1 to +1).

questions.q: A student proposes the following set of four quantum numbers for an electron: n = 4, ℓ = 3, m_ℓ = 4, mₛ = +½. Determine whether this set is VALID or INVALID. If it is invalid, state clearly which rule is broken and correct the erroneous value.
questions.answer:
INVALID — the rule −ℓ ≤ mℓ ≤ +ℓ is broken.

Rule: - ell ≤ mell ≤ + ell. Given ell = 3: - 3 ≤ mell ≤ + 3. But mell = 4 → INVALID

Correction: mℓ must be one of −3, ..., 0, ..., +3 (e.g. mℓ = +3).

questions.q: A student proposes the following set of four quantum numbers for an electron: n = 5, ℓ = 1, m_ℓ = -1, mₛ = +1. Determine whether this set is VALID or INVALID. If it is invalid, state clearly which rule is broken and correct the erroneous value.
questions.answer:
INVALID — the spin quantum number can only take the value +½ or −½.

ms = + 1 → not a permitted value → INVALID

Correction: ms must be changed to +½ or −½ (the two spin states of an electron).

questions.q: A student proposes the following set of four quantum numbers for an electron: n = 1, ℓ = 0, m_ℓ = 0, mₛ = -½. Determine whether this set is VALID or INVALID. If it is invalid, state clearly which rule is broken and correct the erroneous value.
questions.answer:
VALID.

ell ≤ n - 1: 0 ≤ 0 ✓ - ell ≤ mell ≤ + ell: - 0 ≤ 0 ≤ + 0 ✓

ms = -½, which is one of the two permitted values (+½ or −½). All four quantum numbers obey the rules, so this is a physically allowed description of an electron.

questions.q: A student proposes the following set of four quantum numbers for an electron: n = 6, ℓ = 4, m_ℓ = -3, mₛ = +½. Determine whether this set is VALID or INVALID. If it is invalid, state clearly which rule is broken and correct the erroneous value.
questions.answer:
VALID.

ell ≤ n - 1: 4 ≤ 5 ✓ - ell ≤ mell ≤ + ell: - 4 ≤ - 3 ≤ + 4 ✓

ms = +½, which is one of the two permitted values (+½ or −½). All four quantum numbers obey the rules, so this is a physically allowed description of an electron.

questions.q: A student proposes the following set of four quantum numbers for an electron: n = 0, ℓ = 0, m_ℓ = 0, mₛ = +½. Determine whether this set is VALID or INVALID. If it is invalid, state clearly which rule is broken and correct the erroneous value.
questions.answer:
INVALID — n must be a positive, non-zero integer (n = 1, 2, 3, ...).

n = 0 → not permitted → INVALID

Correction: the smallest allowed value is n = 1 (with ℓ = 0, mℓ = 0).

questions.q: A student proposes the following set of four quantum numbers for an electron: n = 4, ℓ = 2, m_ℓ = -1, mₛ = -½. Determine whether this set is VALID or INVALID. If it is invalid, state clearly which rule is broken and correct the erroneous value.
questions.answer:
VALID.

ell ≤ n - 1: 2 ≤ 3 ✓ - ell ≤ mell ≤ + ell: - 2 ≤ - 1 ≤ + 2 ✓

ms = -½, which is one of the two permitted values (+½ or −½). All four quantum numbers obey the rules, so this is a physically allowed description of an electron.

questions.q: Calculate (i) the number of orbitals and (ii) the maximum number of electrons that can be accommodated in the shell with principal quantum number n = 2.
questions.answer:
n² = 2² = 4 orbitals | 2n² = 2( 2 )² = 8 electrons

So the n = 2 shell has 4 orbitals and can hold a maximum of 8 electrons.

questions.q: Calculate (i) the number of orbitals and (ii) the maximum number of electrons that can be accommodated in the shell with principal quantum number n = 5.
questions.answer:
n² = 5² = 25 orbitals | 2n² = 2( 5 )² = 50 electrons

So the n = 5 shell has 25 orbitals and can hold a maximum of 50 electrons.

questions.q: Calculate (i) the number of orbitals and (ii) the maximum number of electrons that can be accommodated in the shell with principal quantum number n = 6.
questions.answer:
n² = 6² = 36 orbitals | 2n² = 2( 6 )² = 72 electrons

So the n = 6 shell has 36 orbitals and can hold a maximum of 72 electrons.

questions.q: For the n = 4 shell, ℓ can take the values 0, 1, 2 and 3 (s, p, d, f). By calculating the number of orbitals contributed by each subshell (2ℓ + 1) and summing them, show that the total number of orbitals in the n = 4 shell is indeed equal to n².
questions.answer:
Using 2ℓ + 1 for each subshell: ℓ = 0 (s) gives 1 orbital, ℓ = 1 (p) gives 3, ℓ = 2 (d) gives 5, and ℓ = 3 (f) gives 7 orbitals.

1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16 | n² = 4² = 16

Since both methods give 16, this confirms that the total number of orbitals in a shell equals n².

questions.q: A certain shell can hold a maximum of 98 electrons. Determine the principal quantum number, n, of this shell.
A shell is found to contain a total of 64 orbitals. Determine the principal quantum number, n, of this shell.
Identify the shell (state its principal quantum number, n) whose maximum electron capacity is 18 electrons, and name the subshells (s, p, d, ...) that this shell contains.
questions.answer:
2n² = 18 → n² = 9 → n = 3

For n = 3, ℓ = 0, 1, 2 → the shell contains the 3s, 3p and 3d subshells.

questions.q: Calculate the maximum number of electrons that the n = 3 shell and the n = 4 shell can each hold, and hence determine how many more electrons the n = 4 shell can accommodate compared to the n = 3 shell.
questions.answer:
2( 3 )² = 18 | 2( 4 )² = 32 | 32 - 18 = 14

The n = 4 shell can hold 14 more electrons than the n = 3 shell.

questions.q: A shell contains 100 orbitals in total. Determine its principal quantum number, n, and calculate the maximum number of electrons it can hold.
The difference in the maximum electron capacity between two consecutive shells, n and (n + 1), is found to be 22 electrons. Identify the two values of n, showing your working.
questions.answer:
Let the maximum capacities be 2n² and 2(n + 1)². By trial using consecutive integers:

2( 5 )² = 50 | 2( 6 )² = 72 | 72 - 50 = 22

Therefore the two shells are n = 5 and n = 6.

questions.q: Write the complete set of four quantum numbers (n, ℓ, mℓ, ms) for every electron in a 3p⁵ configuration. Present your answer as a table (applying Hund's rule and the Pauli exclusion principle), and state how many of these electrons are unpaired.
questions.answer:
Electron 1: n=3, ℓ=1, mℓ=-1, ms=+½
Electron 2: n=3, ℓ=1, mℓ=0, ms=+½
Electron 3: n=3, ℓ=1, mℓ=1, ms=+½
Electron 4: n=3, ℓ=1, mℓ=-1, ms=-½
Electron 5: n=3, ℓ=1, mℓ=0, ms=-½

Number of unpaired electrons = 1.

questions.q: Write the complete set of four quantum numbers (n, ℓ, mℓ, ms) for every electron in a 4d³ configuration. Present your answer as a table (applying Hund's rule and the Pauli exclusion principle), and state how many of these electrons are unpaired.
questions.answer:
Electron 1: n=4, ℓ=2, mℓ=-2, ms=+½
Electron 2: n=4, ℓ=2, mℓ=-1, ms=+½
Electron 3: n=4, ℓ=2, mℓ=0, ms=+½

Number of unpaired electrons = 3.

questions.q: Write the complete set of four quantum numbers (n, ℓ, mℓ, ms) for every electron in a 5p⁴ configuration. Present your answer as a table (applying Hund's rule and the Pauli exclusion principle), and state how many of these electrons are unpaired.
questions.answer:
Electron 1: n=5, ℓ=1, mℓ=-1, ms=+½
Electron 2: n=5, ℓ=1, mℓ=0, ms=+½
Electron 3: n=5, ℓ=1, mℓ=1, ms=+½
Electron 4: n=5, ℓ=1, mℓ=-1, ms=-½

Number of unpaired electrons = 2.

questions.q: Write the complete set of four quantum numbers (n, ℓ, mℓ, ms) for every electron in a 3d⁷ configuration. Present your answer as a table (applying Hund's rule and the Pauli exclusion principle), and state how many of these electrons are unpaired.
questions.answer:
Electron 1: n=3, ℓ=2, mℓ=-2, ms=+½
Electron 2: n=3, ℓ=2, mℓ=-1, ms=+½
Electron 3: n=3, ℓ=2, mℓ=0, ms=+½
Electron 4: n=3, ℓ=2, mℓ=1, ms=+½
Electron 5: n=3, ℓ=2, mℓ=2, ms=+½
Electron 6: n=3, ℓ=2, mℓ=-2, ms=-½
Electron 7: n=3, ℓ=2, mℓ=-1, ms=-½

Number of unpaired electrons = 3.

questions.q: Write the complete set of four quantum numbers (n, ℓ, mℓ, ms) for every electron in a 4f³ configuration. Present your answer as a table (applying Hund's rule and the Pauli exclusion principle), and state how many of these electrons are unpaired.
questions.answer:
Electron 1: n=4, ℓ=3, mℓ=-3, ms=+½
Electron 2: n=4, ℓ=3, mℓ=-2, ms=+½
Electron 3: n=4, ℓ=3, mℓ=-1, ms=+½

Number of unpaired electrons = 3.

questions.q: Write the complete set of four quantum numbers (n, ℓ, mℓ, ms) for every electron in a 4p³ configuration. Present your answer as a table (applying Hund's rule and the Pauli exclusion principle), and state how many of these electrons are unpaired.
questions.answer:
Electron 1: n=4, ℓ=1, mℓ=-1, ms=+½
Electron 2: n=4, ℓ=1, mℓ=0, ms=+½
Electron 3: n=4, ℓ=1, mℓ=1, ms=+½

Number of unpaired electrons = 3.

questions.q: Write the complete set of four quantum numbers (n, ℓ, mℓ, ms) for every electron in a 3s² configuration. Present your answer as a table (applying Hund's rule and the Pauli exclusion principle), and state how many of these electrons are unpaired.
questions.answer:
Electron 1: n=3, ℓ=0, mℓ=0, ms=+½
Electron 2: n=3, ℓ=0, mℓ=0, ms=-½

Number of unpaired electrons = 0.

questions.q: Write the complete set of four quantum numbers (n, ℓ, mℓ, ms) for every electron in a 6s¹ configuration. Present your answer as a table (applying Hund's rule and the Pauli exclusion principle), and state how many of these electrons are unpaired.
questions.answer:
Electron 1: n=6, ℓ=0, mℓ=0, ms=+½

Number of unpaired electrons = 1.

questions.q: Write the full ground-state electron configuration (spdf notation) of a nitrogen atom, N (Z = 7).
questions.answer: 1s² 2s² 2p³

questions.q: Write the ground-state electron configuration of a silicon atom, Si (Z = 14), in (i) full spdf notation and (ii) noble-gas-core notation.
questions.answer:
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p²

[Ne] 3s² 3p²

questions.q: Write the noble-gas-core electron configuration of a potassium atom, K (Z = 19), and explain why the 19th electron enters the 4s orbital rather than the 3d orbital.
questions.answer:
[Ar] 4s¹

The 4s orbital, although belonging to a higher principal quantum number, has a lower energy than the 3d orbital for K. By the Aufbau principle, electrons occupy the lowest-energy available orbital first; since 4s \< 3d in energy at this point, the 19th electron fills the 4s orbital before any electron enters 3d.

questions.q: Write the ground-state electron configuration of an iron atom, Fe (Z = 26), in (i) full spdf notation and (ii) noble-gas-core notation.
questions.answer:
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 3d⁶

[Ar] 4s² 3d⁶

questions.q: Write the ground-state electron configuration of a zinc atom, Zn (Z = 30), in (i) full spdf notation and (ii) noble-gas-core notation.
questions.answer:
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 3d¹⁰

[Ar] 4s² 3d¹⁰

questions.q: Write the noble-gas-core electron configuration of a bromine atom, Br (Z = 35).
questions.answer: [Ar] 4s² 3d¹⁰ 4p⁵

questions.q: Write the ground-state electron configuration of a strontium atom, Sr (Z = 38), in (i) full spdf notation and (ii) noble-gas-core notation.
questions.answer:
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 3d¹⁰ 4p⁶ 5s²

[Kr] 5s²

questions.q: Write the noble-gas-core electron configuration of a zirconium atom, Zr (Z = 40).
questions.answer: [Kr] 5s² 4d²

questions.q: Write the noble-gas-core electron configuration of the Fe²⁺ ion (Fe, Z = 26). Explain which sub-shell loses electrons first when a neutral transition-metal atom is ionised to form a cation.
questions.answer:
[Ar] 3d⁶

For transition metals, electrons are removed from the outermost s subshell before the inner d subshell, because once the 3d subshell begins to fill, it becomes lower in energy than 4s in the ion. Fe is [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶; removing 2 electrons therefore empties the 4s orbital first, leaving [Ar] 3d⁶.

questions.q: Write the noble-gas-core electron configuration of the Fe³⁺ ion (Fe, Z = 26), and explain why the Fe³⁺ ion is particularly stable.
questions.answer:
[Ar] 3d⁵

Both 4s electrons are removed first, followed by one 3d electron, giving [Ar] 3d⁵. This configuration is especially stable because the 3d subshell is exactly half-filled (one electron in each of the five 3d orbitals with parallel spin), which is a lower-energy, more stable arrangement by the rule of stability.

questions.q: Write the noble-gas-core electron configuration of the Ti²⁺ ion (Ti, Z = 22).
questions.answer: [Ar] 3d²

questions.q: Write the electron configuration of the S²⁻ ion (S, Z = 16) in (i) full spdf notation and (ii) noble-gas-core notation, and state which noble gas it is isoelectronic with.
questions.answer:
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶

[Ne] 3s² 3p⁶

S²⁻ has 18 electrons, the same configuration and electron count as a neutral argon (Ar) atom — the two species are isoelectronic.

questions.q: Write the electron configuration of the O²⁻ ion (O, Z = 8) in full spdf notation, and state which noble gas it is isoelectronic with.
questions.answer:
1s² 2s² 2p⁶

O²⁻ has 10 electrons, the same configuration and electron count as a neutral neon (Ne) atom — the two species are isoelectronic.

questions.q: Write the electron configurations of the Na⁺ ion (Na, Z = 11) and the F⁻ ion (F, Z = 9). Explain, using the term 'isoelectronic', why these two ions have identical electron configurations even though they come from different elements.
questions.answer:
Na⁺: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶

F⁻: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶

Na (Z = 11) loses 1 electron to form Na⁺ (10 electrons); F (Z = 9) gains 1 electron to form F⁻ (10 electrons). Both ions therefore have exactly 10 electrons arranged as 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ — the same configuration as neutral neon. Species with identical electron configurations (the same number and arrangement of electrons), regardless of their nuclear charge, are described as isoelectronic.

questions.q: Draw (describe using ↑ / ↓ notation) the orbital box diagram for the 2p subshell of a nitrogen atom, N (Z = 7), and state whether the atom is paramagnetic or diamagnetic. Justify your answer.
questions.answer:
Full configuration: 1s² 2s² 2p³. Orbital box diagram for 2p³ (applying Hund's rule — one electron enters each degenerate orbital before pairing begins):

mℓ = -1: [↑] mℓ = 0: [↑] mℓ = +1: [↑]

All three 2p electrons are unpaired (parallel spins in separate orbitals). Since the atom contains unpaired electrons, nitrogen is PARAMAGNETIC.

questions.q: A magnesium atom, Mg (Z = 12), has the configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s². Draw the orbital box diagram for the 3s subshell and state whether Mg is paramagnetic or diamagnetic.
questions.answer:
mℓ = 0: [↑↓]

Every subshell in Mg (1s, 2s, 2p, 3s) is completely filled, so all electrons are paired. Since there are no unpaired electrons, magnesium is DIAMAGNETIC.

questions.q: The O²⁻ ion (O, Z = 8) has the configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶. Draw the orbital box diagram for the 2p subshell of O²⁻ and determine whether this ion is paramagnetic or diamagnetic.
questions.answer:
mℓ = -1: [↑↓] mℓ = 0: [↑↓] mℓ = +1: [↑↓]

All three 2p orbitals are completely filled (2 electrons each, paired). With no unpaired electrons, the O²⁻ ion is DIAMAGNETIC.

questions.q: The Fe²⁺ ion (Fe, Z = 26) has the noble-gas-core configuration [Ar] 3d⁶. Draw the orbital box diagram for the 3d subshell and determine whether Fe²⁺ is paramagnetic or diamagnetic.
questions.answer:
mℓ = -2: [↑↓] mℓ = -1: [↑] mℓ = 0: [↑] mℓ = +1: [↑] mℓ = +2: [↑]

Applying Hund's rule, the first 5 electrons singly occupy all five 3d orbitals with parallel spin; the 6th electron must then pair up in the mℓ = −2 orbital. This leaves 4 unpaired electrons (in the mℓ = −1, 0, +1, +2 orbitals). Since unpaired electrons are present, Fe²⁺ is PARAMAGNETIC.

questions.q: A zinc atom, Zn (Z = 30), has the noble-gas-core configuration [Ar] 4s² 3d¹⁰. Draw the orbital box diagrams for the 4s and 3d subshells and determine whether Zn is paramagnetic or diamagnetic.
questions.answer:
4s: mℓ = 0: [↑↓]

3d: mℓ = -2: [↑↓] mℓ = -1: [↑↓] mℓ = 0: [↑↓] mℓ = +1: [↑↓] mℓ = +2: [↑↓]

Both the 4s and 3d subshells are completely filled, so every electron is paired. With no unpaired electrons, zinc is DIAMAGNETIC.

questions.q: The transition element chromium, Cr (Z = 24) does not follow the Aufbau-predicted electron configuration. (a) Write the expected (Aufbau-predicted) noble-gas-core configuration. (b) Write the actual (experimentally observed) configuration. (c) Explain this discrepancy using the rule of stability.
questions.answer:
Expected (Aufbau-predicted):

[Ar] 4s² 3d⁴

Actual (observed):

[Ar] 4s¹ 3d⁵

Cr gains extra stability by having a half-filled 3d subshell (one electron in each of the five 3d orbitals) together with a half-filled (single-electron) 4s orbital. One 4s electron is promoted into the empty 3d orbital to achieve this more stable, lower-energy half-filled arrangement.

questions.q: The transition element copper, Cu (Z = 29) does not follow the Aufbau-predicted electron configuration. (a) Write the expected (Aufbau-predicted) noble-gas-core configuration. (b) Write the actual (experimentally observed) configuration. (c) Explain this discrepancy using the rule of stability.
questions.answer:
Expected (Aufbau-predicted):

[Ar] 4s² 3d⁹

Actual (observed):

[Ar] 4s¹ 3d¹⁰

Cu gains extra stability by having a completely filled 3d subshell (all five 3d orbitals doubly occupied). One 4s electron is promoted into the 3d subshell so that it becomes fully filled, which is a more stable, lower-energy arrangement than a partially filled 3d⁹ subshell.

questions.q: The transition element molybdenum, Mo (Z = 42) does not follow the Aufbau-predicted electron configuration. (a) Write the expected (Aufbau-predicted) noble-gas-core configuration. (b) Write the actual (experimentally observed) configuration. (c) Explain this discrepancy using the rule of stability.
questions.answer:
Expected (Aufbau-predicted):

[Kr] 5s² 4d⁴

Actual (observed):

[Kr] 5s¹ 4d⁵

Mo behaves like Cr (same group): one 5s electron is promoted into the 4d subshell so that 4d becomes exactly half-filled (4d⁵), which — together with the half-filled 5s¹ — is more stable than the predicted 4d⁴ 5s² arrangement.

questions.q: The transition element silver, Ag (Z = 47) does not follow the Aufbau-predicted electron configuration. (a) Write the expected (Aufbau-predicted) noble-gas-core configuration. (b) Write the actual (experimentally observed) configuration. (c) Explain this discrepancy using the rule of stability.
questions.answer:
Expected (Aufbau-predicted):

[Kr] 5s² 4d⁹

Actual (observed):

[Kr] 5s¹ 4d¹⁰

Ag behaves like Cu (same group): one 5s electron is promoted into the 4d subshell so that 4d becomes completely filled (4d¹⁰), which is more stable than the predicted partially filled 4d⁹ arrangement.

questions.q: The transition element palladium, Pd (Z = 46) does not follow the Aufbau-predicted electron configuration. (a) Write the expected (Aufbau-predicted) noble-gas-core configuration. (b) Write the actual (experimentally observed) configuration. (c) Explain this discrepancy using the rule of stability.
questions.answer:
Expected (Aufbau-predicted):

[Kr] 5s² 4d⁸

Actual (observed):

[Kr] 4d¹⁰

Pd is an even more extreme exception: BOTH 5s electrons are promoted into the 4d subshell, emptying 5s completely (5s⁰) and completely filling 4d (4d¹⁰). A fully filled 4d subshell together with an empty 5s subshell is more stable overall than the predicted partially-filled 4d⁸ 5s² arrangement.
